Key enablers discussed in the canonical 6G vision include waveform design, novel multiple access, advanced channel coding, cell-free massive MIMO, network slicing, and cloud–fog–edge computing [Source 1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11432-020-2955-6).

For the IoI, the most consequential shift is the move from "connected things" to "connected intelligence", wherein the radio interface itself becomes programmable and AI-driven [Source 2](https://doi.org/10.1109/jsac.2021.3126076).
Edge intelligence (EI) is broadly defined as the embedding of model training and inference capabilities at the network edge [Source 2](https://doi.org/10.1109/jsac.2021.3126076).

The 6G Edge Intelligence white paper identifies five functional domains where EI is critical: edge computing infrastructure, data and network management, software development for edge, real-time and distributed training of ML/AI, and security, privacy, and pricing [Source 8](http://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14850).

A complementary survey frames *Intelligence Edge Computing* (IEC) as a 5G-and-beyond backbone that supports autonomous vehicles, AR/VR, big-data analytics, and customer-oriented services [Source 9](https://doi.org/10.3390/fi13050118).

A foundational EI reference is the "edge intelligence" framework proposed in [Source 12](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Edge-Intelligence%3A-Paving-the-Last-Mile-of-With-Zhou-Chen/928cd808aba140ec298508df87c5579811ff2f41), which formalizes the training and inference pipelines running across the cloud–edge–device continuum.

Within the radio access network (RAN), edge intelligence has been proposed as a means to virtualize and orchestrate AI workloads alongside RAN functions; for example, the Edge Intelligent Radio Access Network Architecture (EIRA) uses a Markov-chain-based RIC scheduler to allocate intelligence elements across virtualized RAN functions [Source 15](https://doi.org/10.1155/2022/4955498).

The ISAC vision articulated in [Source 3](https://doi.org/10.1109/jsac.2022.3156632) describes a perceptive 6G network in which the same waveforms and infrastructure are used for both data transmission and environmental sensing—enabling applications such as joint communication–radar, indoor localization, gesture recognition, and human activity detection.

By extracting intelligence directly from the radio channel, ISAC reduces the need for dedicated sensors and provides a continuous, network-level perception layer that feeds downstream AI models [Source 3](https://doi.org/10.1109/jsac.2022.3156632).

Edge AI is the most studied instantiation: the canonical edge-AI framework in [Source 2](https://doi.org/10.1109/jsac.2021.3126076) identifies six axes of optimization—wireless-aware model design, split/federated learning, on-device adaptation, and trustworthy inference—and shows that co-designing communication and learning yields multiplicative gains over isolated optimizations.

The 6G white paper on edge intelligence further specifies how distributed ML/AI training can be made real-time, secure, and privacy-preserving across heterogeneous edges [Source 8](http://arxiv.org/abs/2004.14850).

The DITEN survey [Source 5](https://doi.org/10.1109/ojcoms.2022.3197811) defines DITEN as the integration of MEC and digital twins, providing continuous network-state monitoring and supporting centralized optimization of routing, resource management, and caching.

Key design dimensions include DT modeling, updating, deployment, and the resolution at which the twin is synchronized with its physical counterpart [Source 5](https://doi.org/10.1109/ojcoms.2022.3197811).

The industrial perspective in [Source 6](https://doi.com/10.1016/j.jnca.2021.103309) extends this view to Industry 4.0, where DT-enabled smart industries rely on the convergence of IIoT, edge/cloud computing, and advanced analytics.

From the AI side, [Source 7](https://doi.org/10.1109/mcom.001.2001237) frames the DT as the embodiment of a cyber-physical system (CPS) and identifies concrete AI agents operating at the application and infrastructure levels—for example, a movement-prediction agent validated on a robotic-arm twin.

Blockchain has been proposed as a substrate for auditable model and data exchange, complemented by multi-access edge computing (MEC) for low-latency task execution; for example, [Source 16](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01156) analyzes how these two technologies jointly enhance the autonomy of distributed robotic systems by enabling tamper-proof task logs and decentralized coordination.

evidence.title: Towards 6G wireless communication networks: vision, enabling technologies, and new paradigm shifts
evidence.abstract: Abstract The fifth generation (5G) wireless communication networks are being deployed worldwide from 2020 and more capabilities are in the process of being standardized, such as mass connectivity, ultra-reliability, and guaranteed low latency. However, 5G will not meet all requirements of the future in 2030 and beyond, and sixth generation (6G) wireless communication networks are expected to provide global coverage, enhanced spectral/energy/cost efficiency, better intelligence level and security, etc. To meet these requirements, 6G networks will rely on new enabling technologies, i.e., air interface and transmission technologies and novel network architecture, such as waveform design, multiple access, channel coding schemes, multi-antenna technologies, network slicing, cell-free architecture, and cloud/fog/edge computing. Our vision on 6G is that it will have four new paradigm shifts. First, to satisfy the requirement of global coverage, 6G will not be limited to terrestrial communication networks, which will need to be complemented with non-terrestrial networks such as satellite and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) communication networks, thus achieving a space-air-ground-sea integrated communication network. Second, all spectra will be fully explored to further increase data rates and connection density, including the sub-6 GHz, millimeter wave (mmWave), terahertz (THz), and optical frequency bands. Third, facing the big datasets generated by the use of extremely heterogeneous networks, diverse communication scenarios, large numbers of antennas, wide bandwidths, and new service requirements, 6G networks will enable a new range of smart applications with the aid of artificial intelligence (AI) and big data technologies. Fourth, network security will have to be strengthened when developing 6G networks. This article provides a comprehensive survey of recent advances and future trends in these four aspects. Clearly, 6G with additional technical requirements beyond those of 5G will enable faster and further communications to the extent that the boundary between physical and cyber worlds disappears.

We also outline several key reflections and future research challenges and directions to facilitate industrial DT’s adoption.

By embedding model training and inference capabilities into the network edge, edge AI stands out as a disruptive technology for 6G to seamlessly integrate sensing, communication, computation, and intelligence, thereby improving the efficiency, effectiveness, privacy, and security of 6G networks. In this paper, we shall provide our vision for scalable and trustworthy edge AI systems with integrated design of wireless communication strategies and decentralized machine learning models. New design principles of wireless networks, service-driven resource allocation optimization methods, as well as a holistic end-to-end system architecture to support edge AI will be described. evidence.title: Communications in the 6G Era
evidence.abstract: The focus of wireless research is increasingly shifting toward 6G as 5G deployments get underway. At this juncture, it is essential to establish a vision of future communications to provide guidance for that research. In this paper, we attempt to paint a broad picture of communication needs and technologies in the timeframe of 6G. The future of connectivity is in the creation of digital twin worlds that are a true representation of the physical and biological worlds at every spatial and time instant, unifying our experience across these physical, biological and digital worlds. Second, a comprehensive design of DITEN is devised, including the DT modeling/updating, DT deployment, key issues, and enabling technologies. Then, the typical applications of DITEN towards 6G are provided, including the Internet of Things (IoT), vehicular network, space-air-groud integrated network (SAGIN), healthcare, wireless systems, and other applications, along with the design of DITEN in each application, such as DT modeling, DT association, incentive mechanisms, and so on. Finally, challenges and open issues are discussed.

evidence.title: Towards 6G wireless communication networks: vision, enabling technologies, and new paradigm shifts
evidence.abstract: Abstract The fifth generation (5G) wireless communication networks are being deployed worldwide from 2020 and more capabilities are in the process of being standardized, such as mass connectivity, ultra-reliability, and guaranteed low latency. However, 5G will not meet all requirements of the future in 2030 and beyond, and sixth generation (6G) wireless communication networks are expected to provide global coverage, enhanced spectral/energy/cost efficiency, better intelligence level and security, etc. To meet these requirements, 6G networks will rely on new enabling technologies, i.e., air interface and transmission technologies and novel network architecture, such as waveform design, multiple access, channel coding schemes, multi-antenna technologies, network slicing, cell-free architecture, and cloud/fog/edge computing. Our vision on 6G is that it will have four new paradigm shifts. First, to satisfy the requirement of global coverage, 6G will not be limited to terrestrial communication networks, which will need to be complemented with non-terrestrial networks such as satellite and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) communication networks, thus achieving a space-air-ground-sea integrated communication network. Second, all spectra will be fully explored to further increase data rates and connection density, including the sub-6 GHz, millimeter wave (mmWave), terahertz (THz), and optical frequency bands. Third, facing the big datasets generated by the use of extremely heterogeneous networks, diverse communication scenarios, large numbers of antennas, wide bandwidths, and new service requirements, 6G networks will enable a new range of smart applications with the aid of artificial intelligence (AI) and big data technologies. Fourth, network security will have to be strengthened when developing 6G networks. This article provides a comprehensive survey of recent advances and future trends in these four aspects. Clearly, 6G with additional technical requirements beyond those of 5G will enable faster and further communications to the extent that the boundary between physical and cyber worlds disappears.

evidence.title: Industrial digital twins at the nexus of NextG wireless networks and computational intelligence: A survey
evidence.abstract: By amalgamating recent communication and control technologies, computing and data analytics techniques, and modular manufacturing, Industry 4.0 promotes integrating cyber–physical worlds through cyber–physical systems (CPS) and digital twin (DT) for monitoring, optimization, and prognostics of industrial processes. A DT enables interaction with the digital image of the industrial physical objects/processes to simulate, analyze, and control their real-time operation. DT is rapidly diffusing in numerous industries with the interdisciplinary advances in the industrial Internet of things (IIoT), edge and cloud computing, machine learning, artificial intelligence, and advanced data analytics. However, the existing literature lacks in identifying and discussing the role and requirements of these technologies in DT-enabled industries from the communication and computing perspective. In this article, we first present the functional aspects, appeal, and innovative use of DT in smart industries. Then, we elaborate on this perspective by systematically reviewing and reflecting on recent research trends in next-generation (NextG) wireless technologies (e.g., 5G-and-Beyond networks) and design tools, and current computational intelligence paradigms (e.g., edge and cloud computing-enabled data analytics, federated learning). Moreover, we discuss the DT deployment strategies at different communication layers to meet the monitoring and control requirements of industrial applications. We also outline several key reflections and future research challenges and directions to facilitate industrial DT’s adoption.
